summary.text: The gamma recurrence rewrites the ratio using ordinary factorials and an odd-step product; splitting these into their multiples of \(p\) and their \(p\)-coprime parts reduces the claim to congruences for shifted blocks of reduced residues modulo \(p^r\). Pairing \(e\) with \(p^r-e\), together with the vanishing modulo \(p^r\) of the reciprocal-square sum over units, makes every such block invariant modulo \(p^{3r}\); the resulting product identity then yields the desired divisibility after cancelling a factor coprime to \(p\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(m)=\frac{(15m)!\,\Gamma(5m/2+1)\,(2m)!}
 {\Gamma(15m/2+1)\,(6m)!\,(5m)!\,m!}.
\]
Thus the symbols \((5m/2)!\) and \((15m/2)!\) in the sequence definition have their gamma-function meaning.

We prove the following precise statement. Let \(p\geq 5\) be prime and let \(n,r>0\). If the two real numbers \(a(np^r)\) and \(a(np^{r-1})\) are integers, then
\[
a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\]
This is exactly the asserted supercongruence whenever the relevant terms of the sequence are integer-valued.

Throughout the proof put
\[
q=p^r.
\]
Notice that \(q\) is odd and that \(2\) and \(3\) are units modulo \(q\).

## 1. A reciprocal-square cancellation

Let
\[
U=\{e:1\leq e\leq q-1,\ p\nmid e\}.
\]
These are precisely the standard integer representatives of the units modulo \(q\). We first show
\[
\sum_{e\in U}e^{-2}=0\pmod q. \tag{1}
\]
Here and below inverses in such formulas are taken in \(\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z\).

Indeed, first sum the squares of all units modulo \(q\), writing
\[
S=\sum_{u\in(\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z)^\times}u^2.
\]
Multiplication by \(2\) permutes the units, so
\[
S=\sum_u(2u)^2=4S.
\]
Consequently \(3S=0\). Since \(3\) is invertible modulo \(q\), \(S=0\). Inversion also permutes the group of units, and hence
\[
\sum_u u^{-2}=\sum_u u^2=0.
\]
Representing the units by the elements of \(U\) proves (1).

We will also need the corresponding sum over the lower half of the representatives. Set
\[
L=\{e:1\leq e\leq (q-1)/2,\ p\nmid e\}.
\]
The involution \(e\mapsto q-e\) pairs the elements of \(U\), with exactly one member of each pair in \(L\). Moreover,
\[
(q-e)^{-2}=(-e)^{-2}=e^{-2}\pmod q.
\]
Thus (1) becomes
\[
0=2\sum_{e\in L}e^{-2}\pmod q.
\]
As \(2\) is invertible modulo \(q\),
\[
\sum_{e\in L}e^{-2}=0\pmod q. \tag{2}
\]

## 2. Cubic congruences for complete \(p\)-free blocks

We prove two block congruences. For every nonnegative integer \(c\),
\[
\prod_{e\in U}(cq+e)\equiv\prod_{e\in U}e\pmod {q^3}, \tag{3}
\]
and
\[
\prod_{e\in U}(cq+2e)\equiv\prod_{e\in U}2e\pmod {q^3}. \tag{4}
\]

We use the elementary product expansion
\[
\prod_{i\in T}(b_i+\delta)
\equiv
\prod_{i\in T}b_i+
\delta\sum_{i\in T}\prod_{j\in T\setminus\{i\}}b_j
\pmod {\delta^2}. \tag{5}
\]
This follows simply by expanding the product: the displayed terms are those in which \(\delta\) is chosen zero or one time, while every omitted term contains at least two factors \(\delta\). Equivalently, it follows by induction on the size of \(T\).

To prove (3), pair the factors indexed by \(e\) and \(q-e\), with \(e\in L\). Their product is
\[
(cq+e)(cq+q-e)
=e(q-e)+c(c+1)q^2.
\]
Set
\[
b_e=e(q-e),\qquad \delta=c(c+1)q^2.
\]
Thus the left side of (3) is \(\prod_{e\in L}(b_e+\delta)\), and its right side is \(\prod_{e\in L}b_e\).

In (5), \(\delta^2\) is divisible by \(q^4\), hence by \(q^3\). It remains to show that
\[
D:=\sum_{e\in L}\prod_{e'\in L\setminus\{e\}}b_{e'}
\]
is divisible by \(q\), because then \(\delta D\) is divisible by \(q^3\). Modulo \(q\),
\[
b_e=e(q-e)\equiv-e^2.
\]
Every \(e\in L\) is a unit modulo \(q\), so every \(b_e\) is also a unit there. Therefore
\[
D\equiv
\left(\prod_{e\in L}b_e\right)
\left(\sum_{e\in L}b_e^{-1}\right)
\equiv
-\left(\prod_{e\in L}b_e\right)
\left(\sum_{e\in L}e^{-2}\right)
\equiv0\pmod q
\]
by (2). Formula (5) now proves (3).

The proof of (4) is identical after pairing \(e\) with \(q-e\). This time
\[
(cq+2e)(cq+2(q-e))
=4e(q-e)+c(c+2)q^2.
\]
Set \(b_e=4e(q-e)\) and \(\delta=c(c+2)q^2\). Again \(\delta^2\) is divisible by \(q^3\). Modulo \(q\), \(b_e\equiv-4e^2\), and \(4\) is a unit. Hence
\[
\sum_{e\in L}b_e^{-1}
\]
is a fixed unit multiple of \(\sum_{e\in L}e^{-2}\), and is therefore zero modulo \(q\) by (2). The same expansion proves (4).

## 3. Products of all \(p\)-free factors

For \(N\geq0\), define
\[
G_p(N)=\prod_{\substack{1\leq e\leq N\\p\nmid e}}e.
\]
Dividing the interval \([1,Kq]\) into \(K\) consecutive blocks of length \(q\), and applying (3) to every block, gives
\[
G_p(Kq)\equiv G_p(q)^K\pmod {q^3}. \tag{6}
\]
The endpoint \(q\) itself is omitted because it is divisible by \(p\), so the basic block product is indeed
\[
G_p(q)=\prod_{e\in U}e.
\]
More explicitly, the \((c+1)\)-st block contributes
\(\prod_{e\in U}(cq+e)\), which is congruent to \(G_p(q)\) by (3); multiplying these congruences proves (6).

We also need a shifted product with step two. Define
\[
B_p(C,K)=
\prod_{\substack{1\leq j\leq Kq\\p\nmid j}}(Cq+2j).
\]
Its \((c+1)\)-st block, after writing \(j=cq+e\), contributes
\[
\prod_{e\in U}((C+2c)q+2e),
\]
which is congruent by (4) to \(\prod_{e\in U}2e\). Therefore
\[
B_p(C,K)\equiv
\left(\prod_{e\in U}2e\right)^K
\pmod {q^3}. \tag{7}
\]

The number of elements of \(U\) is
\[
|U|=q-p^{r-1}. \tag{8}
\]
Indeed, among \(1,\dots,q-1\), the multiples of \(p\) are
\(p,2p,\dots,(p^{r-1}-1)p\), so there are \(p^{r-1}-1\) of them. Subtracting from \(q-1\) gives (8). Consequently, if
\[
g=G_p(q)=\prod_{e\in U}e,
\]
then
\[
\prod_{e\in U}2e=2^{q-p^{r-1}}g. \tag{9}
\]

## 4. Removing the gamma functions

Define the positive integer
\[
P(m)=\prod_{j=1}^{5m}(5m+2j).
\]
The gamma recurrence \(\Gamma(x+1)=x\Gamma(x)\), iterated \(5m\) times, gives
\[
\Gamma\left(\frac{15m}{2}+1\right)
=
\Gamma\left(\frac{5m}{2}+1\right)
\prod_{i=0}^{5m-1}\left(\frac{5m}{2}+1+i\right).
\]
Since
\[
\prod_{i=0}^{5m-1}\left(\frac{5m}{2}+1+i\right)
=2^{-5m}\prod_{j=1}^{5m}(5m+2j)
=\frac{P(m)}{2^{5m}},
\]
we obtain
\[
\Gamma\left(\frac{15m}{2}+1\right)
=
\Gamma\left(\frac{5m}{2}+1\right)\frac{P(m)}{2^{5m}}.
\]
All quantities being divided by are nonzero. Substitution into the definition of \(a(m)\) therefore yields the exact identity
\[
a(m)P(m)(6m)!(5m)!m!
=(15m)!(2m)!2^{5m}. \tag{10}
\]
This identity is valid as an equality of real numbers, without any integrality assumption on \(a(m)\).

## 5. Separating the multiples of \(p\)

For every nonnegative integer \(Y\), splitting the factors of \((Yp)!\) according to whether they are divisible by \(p\) gives
\[
(Yp)!=p^Y Y!\,G_p(Yp). \tag{11}
\]
Indeed, the divisible factors are \(p,2p,\dots,Yp\), whose product is \(p^Y Y!\), and the remaining product is \(G_p(Yp)\).

There is an analogous split for \(P(Mp)\). Define
\[
R_p(M)=
\prod_{\substack{1\leq j\leq5Mp\\p\nmid j}}(5Mp+2j).
\]
For the indices divisible by \(p\), write \(j=pk\), where \(1\leq k\leq5M\). Then
\[
5Mp+2j=p(5M+2k).
\]
Thus
\[
P(Mp)=p^{5M}P(M)R_p(M). \tag{12}
\]

Now set
\[
M=np^{r-1},\qquad N=Mp=np^r.
\]
Suppose that
\[
A=a(N),\qquad B=a(M)
\]
are integers. Applying (10) to \(N\) and \(M\) gives the integer identities
\[
A\,P(N)(6N)!(5N)!N!=(15N)!(2N)!2^{5N}, \tag{13}
\]
\[
B\,P(M)(6M)!(5M)!M!=(15M)!(2M)!2^{5M}. \tag{14}
\]
They are integer identities because their left sides contain the assumed integers \(A,B\), while all other factors are positive integers.

Introduce
\[
S_L=R_p(M)G_p(6Mp)G_p(5Mp)G_p(Mp)
\]
and
\[
S_R=2^{5M(p-1)}G_p(15Mp)G_p(2Mp).
\]
Using (11) for the factorials with coefficients \(15,2,6,5,1\), using (12) for \(P(Mp)\), and using
\[
2^{5Mp}=2^{5M}\,2^{5M(p-1)},
\]
we compare (13) and (14). The powers of \(p\) on the numerator side of (13) are
\(p^{15M}p^{2M}=p^{17M}\). On its denominator side, the split of \(P(Mp)\) contributes \(p^{5M}\), while the factorials \((6Mp)!,(5Mp)!,(Mp)!\) contribute \(p^{6M},p^{5M},p^M\), again totaling \(p^{17M}\). All the base factorial and \(P(M)\) factors are those occurring in (14). After multiplying rather than dividing, this comparison gives
\[
A S_L=B S_R. \tag{15}
\]
For completeness, this cancellation can be performed entirely by cross multiplication: substitute (11) and (12) into
\[
(15N)!(2N)!2^{5N}\,S_L\,
 P(M)(6M)!(5M)!M!

after which it becomes exactly
\[
(15M)!(2M)!2^{5M}\,S_R\,
 P(N)(6N)!(5N)!N!.
\]
Equations (13) and (14) then replace the two factorial numerators by the expressions involving \(A\) and \(B\). The common products \(P(N)(6N)!(5N)!N!\) and \(P(M)(6M)!(5M)!M!\) are nonzero, so they may be canceled, yielding (15).

## 6. Comparing \(S_L\) and \(S_R\) modulo \(q^3\)

Because \(Mp=np^r=nq\), formula (6) gives, for every nonnegative integer \(c\),
\[
G_p(cMp)=G_p(cnq)\equiv g^{cn}\pmod {q^3}. \tag{16}
\]
In particular the three ordinary \(G_p\)-factors in \(S_L\) contribute
\[
g^{6n}g^{5n}g^n=g^{12n}. \tag{17}
\]

Also, since \(5Mp=5nq\), the product \(R_p(M)\) can be written as
\[
R_p(M)=
\prod_{\substack{1\leq j\leq5nq\\p\nmid j}}(5nq+2j)
=B_p(5n,5n).
\]
Formula (7) therefore gives
\[
R_p(M)\equiv
\left(\prod_{e\in U}2e\right)^{5n}
\pmod {q^3}. \tag{18}
\]
Combining (17), (18), and (9),
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_L
&\equiv
\left(2^{q-p^{r-1}}g\right)^{5n}g^{12n}\\
&=2^{5n(q-p^{r-1})}g^{17n}
\pmod {q^3}. \tag{19}
\end{aligned}
\]
On the other hand, (16) applied with \(c=15\) and \(c=2\) gives
\[
S_R\equiv2^{5M(p-1)}g^{15n}g^{2n}
=2^{5M(p-1)}g^{17n}
\pmod {q^3}. \tag{20}
\]
Finally,
\[
q-p^{r-1}=p^r-p^{r-1}=p^{r-1}(p-1),
\]
and \(M=np^{r-1}\). Hence
\[
5n(q-p^{r-1})=5M(p-1).
\]
The right sides of (19) and (20) are equal, proving
\[
S_L\equiv S_R\pmod {q^3}. \tag{21}
\]

## 7. Final cancellation

From (15),
\[
(A-B)S_L=B(S_R-S_L). \tag{22}
\]
By (21), \(q^3\mid S_R-S_L\), so (22) implies
\[
q^3\mid (A-B)S_L. \tag{23}
\]
We claim that \(S_L\) is coprime to \(p\). Every factor in each \(G_p\)-product is, by definition, not divisible by \(p\). It remains only to check the factors of \(R_p(M)\). If \(p\nmid j\) but
\[
p\mid 5Mp+2j,
\]
then, since \(p\mid5Mp\), we would have \(p\mid2j\). As \(p\geq5\), \(p\nmid2\), and primality would force \(p\mid j\), a contradiction. Thus all factors of \(R_p(M)\), and hence all factors of \(S_L\), are prime to \(p\).

It follows that \(S_L\) is coprime to \(p^{3r}=q^3\). Euclid's lemma applied to (23) therefore permits cancellation of \(S_L\), giving
\[
p^{3r}=q^3\mid A-B.
\]
Since \(A=a(np^r)\) and \(B=a(np^{r-1})\), this is
\[
a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\]
Equivalently, there is an integer \(c\) with
\[
a(np^r)-a(np^{r-1})=c\,p^{3r},
\]
so the real quotient
\[
\frac{a(np^r)-a(np^{r-1})}{p^{3r}}
\]
is an integer, as required.
